sections.authorBiography: Arthur Conan Doyle was born in Edinburgh on 22 May 1859, studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh, where his teacher Dr. Joseph Bell's powers of observation inspired Sherlock Holmes, and practised as a doctor in Southsea. Holmes first appeared in A Study in Scarlet (1887); the stories in The Strand Magazine from 1891 made him world-famous. Doyle also wrote historical stories and science fiction, served as a volunteer doctor in the Boer War, was knighted in 1902, and in later life became a passionate Spiritualist. He died on 7 July 1930.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “It is fear, Mr. Holmes. It is terror” slowly and put it in my own words: The frightened client says her shivering comes from fear and terror. Next, craft. I notice two short matching sentences, which sound like someone too frightened to speak in long ones. The strongest word is “terror”: Doyle chooses the strongest word available so the mystery opens at full pitch. Then, effect. How does this short speech set up the kind of story this is? My answer: It tells us the detective story will be about danger to a vulnerable person, with Holmes's calm reasoning set against her fear.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Adventure of the Speckled Band.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Adventure of the Speckled Band: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support
middleSchool.text: Supported track: write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Adventure of the Speckled Band teaches about reason and deduction. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Arthur Conan Doyle develops reason and deduction in The Adventure of the Speckled Band. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Arthur Conan Doyle develops reason and deduction across The Adventure of the Speckled Band. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Adventure of the Speckled Band (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of reason and deduction. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of reason and deduction in The Adventure of the Speckled Band. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Arthur Conan Doyle's choices in The Adventure of the Speckled Band (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of reason and deduction, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Adventure of the Speckled Band's treatment of reason and deduction in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on reason and deduction in The Adventure of the Speckled Band that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on reason and deduction in The Adventure of the Speckled Band. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior

prompts.text: Analyze how Arthur Conan Doyle develops reason and deduction across The Adventure of the Speckled Band. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in The Adventure of the Speckled Band and argue how its meaning changes over the story and why that change matters to greed and violence.
Analyze a central character's choices in The Adventure of the Speckled Band. Argue whether the story judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

evidence.sections: at least two parts of the story

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: Roylott is destroyed by the weapon he created. The text makes this visible when it says “Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent” (The Adventure of the Speckled Band, paragraph 245). Holmes drives the snake back, and it kills Roylott; Holmes concludes, "Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent.". A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.
